anatomy.lede: What looks like one animal is a colony: a gas-filled float on top, and beneath it clusters of specialised zooids that feed, sting and breed.

hotspots.label: Float
hotspots.text: The pneumatophore is filled with carbon monoxide and air. Gas-making cells in a gas gland inside the float produce the carbon monoxide.

hotspots.label: Sail crest
hotspots.text: The crest along the top of the float works as a sail. Muscles around the float squeeze it to raise the pressure inside and stand the sail up.

hotspots.label: Feeding zooids
hotspots.text: Under the float hang the gastrozooids, feeding polyps that spread over caught prey and digest it. Upwards of 50 have been seen covering a single 10 cm fish.

hotspots.label: Tentacle
hotspots.text: Each tentacle belongs to a tentacular palpon, a zooid found only in this genus and specialised for making stinging cells. Caught prey is hauled up to the feeding zooids near the float.

stats.label: Share of fish and fish larvae in the diet

body.lede: With no brain, heart or swimming muscles of note, the colony relies on a float, a sail and a curtain of stinging cells.

systems.title: A float that makes its own gas
systems.text: The float holds less carbon monoxide than the floats of other siphonophores, probably because its gas mixes with air through diffusion and exchange.

systems.title: One kind of sting
systems.text: Its stinging capsules are all of a single type, which can only pierce soft-bodied prey. The toxin paralyses fish.

systems.title: A division of labour
systems.text: Unlike other siphonophores, its feeding zooids have no tentacles of their own. Catching prey falls to the tentacular palpons, and eating to the gastrozooids.

genome.lede: Genomes from specimens collected around the world showed that the 'one' man o' war is really several species.

findings.title: A big, repetitive genome
findings.text: The first Physalia genome assembly, made for this global study, measured about 3.33 billion base pairs, with roughly 65% of it made of repeated sequences.

findings.title: Not one species but at least four
findings.text: Whole genomes of 151 samples fell into five distinct lineages that do not appear to interbreed even where they overlap. Four match recognisable body forms, including a newly named species, Physalia minuta.

findings.title: Populations follow the currents
findings.text: Within each species, populations are regional and persist from year to year, with boundaries that line up with prevailing currents and winds.

survival.lede: Drifting at the surface, the colony cannot flee, so its defence is its sting.

tactics.title: A curtain of stings
tactics.text: Tentacles towed by the wind trail far below the float, catching and paralysing fish that brush against them.

tactics.title: A fish that lives among the tentacles
tactics.text: The man-of-war fish, Nomeus gronovii, swims among the tentacles and even feeds on them. It tolerates the venom far better than other fish.

tactics.title: Stings that outlast the colony
tactics.text: The stinging cells stay active after the colony dies, so stranded animals remain dangerous to touch.

life.lede: Much of the man o' war's life cycle happens out of sight, below the surface, and has never been watched directly.

stages.name: Breeding clusters
stages.text: Each colony is either male or female. Its reproductive clusters, called gonodendra, are thought to break away when mature, perhaps swimming down with small jet-propelling bells.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Fertilisation, the egg and the earliest larva have never been observed, and they develop at an unknown depth below the surface.

stages.name: Young larva
stages.text: The smallest larva described is 2 mm long, with a tiny float and a first feeding polyp bearing a tentacle. The sail's left- or right-handed set is fixed this early.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Once its float is big enough, the young colony can ride at the surface. Juveniles have floats about 8–10 cm long and immature breeding clusters.
